common_name: Eight Ball Pomegranate (Cold-Hardy Dwarf Near-Black Pomegranate)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in late winter to early spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Eight Ball is a naturally dwarf, dense, multi-stemmed selection that also performs well in large containers.

directions: Eight Ball was selected from cold-tolerant dwarf pomegranate seedlings for its unusually dark, nearly black fruit skin loaded with anthocyanins, and for a compact, densely twiggy habit that suits hedgerows or large containers as easily as open ground. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil; once established the shrub tolerates drought and Gulf Coast heat with minimal irrigation, and the deep red interior arils ripen to a sweet flavor with softer seeds than many standard-sized pomegranates. Because growth is naturally dense and twiggy, remove crowded interior wood and root suckers each dormant season to keep light reaching developing fruit and to reduce fungal issues in humid weather. Ripe fruit can be left on the plant for a period after coloring without much splitting, giving some slack in harvest scheduling.

common_name: Dente di Cavallo Pomegranate (Italian Horse's-Tooth Heirloom Pomegranate)

planting.note: Plant in full sun on well-drained soil in early-to-mid spring; this Italian heirloom adapts to a wide range of soil types, including heavier or less fertile ground, and is grown throughout mainland Italy as one of the most reliably productive traditional table varieties.

directions: Dente di Cavallo, literally 'horse's tooth,' takes its name from the elongated, angular shape of the fruit's crown, and is one of the traditional heirloom pomegranates grown across Italy for centuries for its dependable, heavy cropping. The medium-to-large fruit has greenish skin blushed with red and encloses sweet, delicately flavored ruby arils that store well after harvest. Plant on well-drained soil in full sun; the variety is noted for tolerating a broad range of soil conditions and for consistent yields even in less-than-ideal ground, making it a forgiving choice for a first Gulf Coast pomegranate planting. Light annual thinning of crowded or crossing branches keeps the canopy open and encourages new fruiting wood.
sources: Preliminary observations on Sicilian pomegranate varieties (ResearchGate)

planting.note: Plant in full sun on well-drained soil in spring; Sumbar originates from the arid Sumbar River valley of Turkmenistan and combines strong cold tolerance with good performance in hot, dry summer conditions typical of the Gulf Coast.

directions: Sumbar is a Central Asian pomegranate selection named for the river valley of its origin in Turkmenistan, prized among cold-climate pomegranate growers as one of the hardiest cultivars available while still producing well-flavored fruit. The pale orange-red skin encloses bright red, soft-seeded arils with a balanced sweet-tart flavor and juice suited to both fresh eating and juicing, ripening earlier in the season than many larger-fruited cultivars. Because its Central Asian steppe origin gives it tolerance for both cold winters and hot, dry summers, it handles Gulf Coast heat with the same ease it shows in cooler climates, provided drainage is good. Plant in full sun and prune lightly each dormant season to remove suckers and open the canopy, since fruit forms on new growth.

common_name: King James Mulberry (Historic English Black Mulberry, syn. 'Chelsea')

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in full sun on well-drained, fertile soil; King James is self-fertile and, like other black mulberries, begins fruiting on relatively young wood.

directions: King James traces its lineage to black mulberries planted in England in the early 1600s under royal patronage for a short-lived silk industry, and old specimens descended from those original plantings are still tended as historic trees; the cultivar is also sold under the synonym 'Chelsea' after the Chelsea Physic Garden. Trees have gnarled, textured bark and heart-shaped leaves that color yellow in fall, and they produce large, richly flavored, deep-purple-black fruit typical of true black mulberry (Morus nigra) — more intensely flavored than white or red mulberry types. Provide fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; established trees tolerate summer heat well but appreciate consistent moisture during fruit development. Because ripe fruit drops and stains heavily, site trees away from patios and walkways, and prune only lightly to maintain shape, since fruiting spurs persist for years on this species.

common_name: Wacissa Mulberry (Florida Heirloom Deep-Purple Sweet Mulberry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Wacissa is self-fertile and, unlike some earlier-budding mulberry selections, tends to stay dormant longer into late winter, reducing the risk of losing an early flush to a late Gulf Coast cold snap.

directions: Wacissa was selected from a long-lived tree found in the small town of Wacissa in the Florida panhandle, and the original tree was still cropping heavily at nearly seventy years old. It bears abundant 1.5-inch, deep purple-black fruit with a rich, sweet flavor often compared to blackberry, on a fast-growing tree that tolerates poor soil and drought once established as well as periods of wet ground. A useful trait for Gulf Coast gardeners is its later, more conservative bud break compared with some other mulberry selections, which helps the spring flush avoid damage from a late frost. Trees can be kept large as shade trees or pruned hard and repeatedly to form a dense hedge, screen, or windbreak.

common_name: Valdosta Mulberry (Extra-Large Black-Fruited Deep South Mulberry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in full sun on well-drained, fertile soil; Valdosta is a vigorous, large-canopied selection best suited to gardens with room for a substantial shade tree rather than a small dooryard planting.

directions: Valdosta originated from a tree near Valdosta, Georgia, close enough to the Gulf Coast climate zone to perform reliably in coastal gardens further south and west. It is best known for unusually long fruit, reaching up to two inches, colored deep black-purple with a rich, sweet flavor, borne on a fast-growing, large-leaved tree with a broad, spreading canopy similar in vigor to other big Deep South mulberry selections. Fruit ripens in a concentrated flush in mid-spring rather than trickling in over weeks, so plan for a short, heavy harvest window. Give it full sun, well-drained fertile soil, and room to spread; established trees need only light structural pruning to remove crossing or damaged limbs.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Gardening Solutions
